CONTEXT.content: Every web app is a conversation between a client (browser, mobile app, another server) and a server. HTTP is the language they speak. When you visit a URL, your browser sends a request; the server processes it and sends back a response with a status code and body.
CONTEXT.analogy: HTTP is like ordering at a restaurant: you place an order (request), the kitchen prepares it (server processing), and the waiter brings it back (response) — or tells you they're out of stock (404).
CONTEXT.productionNote: Every API you build, every bug you debug, every performance issue starts with understanding this request/response cycle.
hints: Think about what information travels in each direction.
What happens if the kitchen never responds?

DECIDE.optionA: Learn HTTP conceptually first — study methods, status codes, headers — then build a server.
DECIDE.optionB: Build a minimal server immediately and learn HTTP by inspecting what it sends and receives.

tradeoffs.A: Stronger mental model before coding; slower initial progress.
tradeoffs.B: Faster hands-on start; may miss concepts until you hit bugs.

hints: Neither is wrong — what matters is your reasoning.

BUILD.goal: Create a minimal HTTP server that responds to GET / with 'Hello, World!' and logs each request's method and path.

tracks.node: Use Node.js http module or Express. Listen on port 3000.
tracks.python: Use Python's http.server or FastAPI. Listen on port 8000.
tracks.typescript: Use Bun.serve or Deno.serve. Listen on port 3000.

acceptance: Server logs show method and path for each request
hints: Start with the smallest possible server — one route, one response.
The issue is usually in how you're binding the port or handling the request object.
Check: are you sending a response for every request? Unanswered requests hang.

criteria: Show curl output with HTTP 200 status
Show server log output for at least 2 different paths
Explain what happens when you curl a path that doesn't exist
hints: Run the acceptance criteria yourself before claiming done.
'It works' without output is not verification.

BREAK.scenario: Something has changed in the deployment. Run your verification again.
BREAK.symptoms: GET / now returns 404. GET /health still works. Logs show requests arriving at / but routing elsewhere.
hints: Form a hypothesis before checking anything.
What's the fastest command to test your hypothesis?
Compare what worked before with what the code does now.

FIX.goal: Identify and fix the routing bug. Explain why it happened.
hints: Trace the request from arrival to response.
Did a route pattern change? Is there an ordering issue?
The bug is in routing — not in HTTP itself.

decisionCallbacks.A: You understood the HTTP contract first. When the routing bug appeared, you likely checked status codes and knew 404 meant 'route not found' — not a server crash.
decisionCallbacks.B: You learned by building. The routing bug taught you that HTTP status codes are part of the contract — 404 vs 500 tell very different stories to clients.
